title: The publisher says "published and verified" about the wrapper while verifying the platform packages, and names only two of three visibility states
description:
Two findings from the 0.9.0 publish, both about the publisher describing an object other than the one it measured.

ONE: the success line names the wrong object. publish-release.mjs prints

  @opum-ai/quest 0.9.0 published and verified (1 check).

from the result of waitForPublished(receipt, version). That helper verifies the SIX PLATFORM PACKAGES against the receipt digests -- it takes the receipt, and the receipt binds the platforms. It does not assert that the wrapper is readable from the registry. So the sentence attributes two different facts about two different objects to the wrapper: that its own publish call returned success, and that the platforms match the receipt.

Measured: the line printed with a genuine exit 0 while two independent anonymous reads disagreed -- a cache-busted packument had no 0.9.0 and https://registry.npmjs.org/@opum-ai%2Fquest/0.9.0 returned HTTP 404. The wrapper appeared about 60 seconds later, so the claim became true; it was not true when printed, and nothing in the output would have distinguished that from a wrapper that never landed.

TWO: staged, never-landed and SLOW are three states, and both the tool and the runbook name two. When quest-linux-arm64 missed the visibility window the publisher reported absent-or-staged and advised --diagnose-staged to separate them. Neither was the answer. The package had landed and was merely slow: --diagnose-staged reported skip, already on the registry at this version. Its evidence was the exact signature the runbook attributes to the 0.7.0 staged incident -- absent from versions, absent from time, time.modified unchanged since the previous release -- so the strongest available read pointed confidently at the wrong one of three states. npm stage list could not adjudicate either, returning E401 for the publishing token.

WHAT IS NOT BROKEN, and should not be changed while fixing this: the gate itself behaved exactly as designed. With one platform package unresolvable the wrapper was withheld, so nothing advertised an optionalDependency that could not resolve. That is the 0.7.0 consumer-facing failure being prevented. The defect is in what the tool SAYS, not in what it does.

acceptanceCriteria.text: The success line distinguishes what was verified from what was published: either it verifies the wrapper is readable before claiming it, or it names the platform packages as the object it verified.
The unresolved-package diagnosis names SLOW as a third possibility alongside staged and never-landed, rather than presenting a binary whose evidence cannot separate the three.

The runbook section on the 0.7.0 staged incident records that the same signature -- absent from versions, absent from time, time.modified unchanged -- was produced by mere propagation lag on 2026-09-18, so a future reader does not treat it as decisive for staging.
Whatever changes, the wrapper is still withheld whenever any platform package does not resolve for a consumer.
